title: Trump Says Saudi Arabia Must Make Friends with Israel to Get a Nuclear Deal
summary: Imagine you want to build a super-cool science project, but your friend says you can only do it if you agree to be friends with someone else. That's kind of what's happening between the U.S., Saudi Arabia, and Israel! President Donald Trump just announced that Saudi Arabia can only get help from the U.S. to build nuclear power plants if it agrees to officially recognize Israel as a country and join something called the Abraham Accords. The Abraham Accords are agreements that help Arab countries and Israel become friends and work together. A few years ago, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain signed them, and later Sudan, Morocco, and Kazakhstan did too. Now Trump wants Saudi Arabia to join the club. The nuclear deal is all about peaceful energy—not weapons. Trump made that clear on his social media site, Truth Social, saying, "The Civil Nuclear Deal (There will be no enrichment of material!)... is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords." That means Saudi Arabia can't use the technology to make nuclear bombs. Some experts worry that even a peaceful nuclear program could lead to dangerous weapons later, especially in the Middle East where tensions are high. But the U.S. Department of Energy says the deal includes strong rules to prevent that. Saudi Arabia's leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, once said his country doesn't want nuclear weapons unless Iran gets them first. So far, Saudi Arabia hasn't responded to Trump's comments. Israel's leaders are happy about Trump's condition, but some Israelis are still nervous about any nuclear program in the region. It's a tricky situation—like trying to balance on a skateboard while holding a glass of water!
why_it_matters: This shows how countries sometimes tie together energy, peace, and friendships, and why one deal could help make a troubled region safer—or risk making it more dangerous.

Article_Structure: WHO: President Donald Trump, Saudi Arabia's leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and Israel.
WHAT: Trump said Saudi Arabia can only get U.S. help for nuclear power plants if it agrees to recognize Israel and join the Abraham Accords.
WHERE: The deal would happen in the Middle East; Trump announced it on his social media site Truth Social.
WHY: To encourage friendship between Arab nations and Israel, and to make sure the nuclear technology is used only for peaceful energy, not bombs.

perspectives.description: They believe tying the nuclear deal to peace with Israel will make the Middle East more stable and stop nuclear weapons from spreading.
Some experts fear that even a peaceful nuclear program could later be used to make dangerous nuclear weapons, especially in a tense region.
